gap: No result ChatGPT got gives a maker's own model-by-model wording for which wireless mode works on which console. EKSA's E900WT page says both its 2.4 GHz dongle mode and its Bluetooth mode are 'NOT compatible with any Xbox', that Bluetooth mode is 'NOT compatible with PS4/PS5', and that the mic does not work on Switch. A sub-$50 'wireless' headset can therefore lose its wireless link (Xbox) or its fallback mode (PlayStation) depending on the console.
standout_why: Rival pages compared: RTINGS wireless-gaming-headsets (cited; only navigation and sidebar loaded, no body text, so no Xbox or Bluetooth statement seen) and RTINGS gaming-headsets-under-50 (same, body did not load). SoundGuys best-cheap-gaming-headset (cited) gives platform lists such as 'easy to use across Xbox, PlayStation, Switch, and PC' but says nothing about why dongles fail on Xbox or about Bluetooth on PS5. Gamecuki (rank 5-6, not cited) already says 'almost none work wirelessly on Xbox, which uses its own wireless standard' and 'Bluetooth ... doesn't work with PS5 or Xbox for game audio'. ChatGPT's third answer also warned that 'many inexpensive wireless gaming headsets won't connect to it [Xbox] wirelessly'. The general mechanism is therefore partly covered. What no rival has: the maker's per-mode wording, the Switch mic limit, and the fact that Logitech's own G435 page lists Xbox while saying LIGHTSPEED runs only on PC, Mac, PS4 and PS5. The Vaagame (cited) page failed with a TLS error, and the PC Gamer body did not load.
decides: It confirms the pick and adds a platform gate. On PC, PS5 or Switch, any of the tri-mode budget picks works over its 2.4 GHz dongle, with Bluetooth only as a phone or PC fallback. On Xbox, none of the sub-$50 2.4 GHz or Bluetooth picks (EKSA E900WT by maker statement; Cloud Jet and E900 BT by retailer listings only) connects wirelessly. Xbox owners need the 3.5 mm cable to the controller, which makes the E900 BT's and Mako BT's included cable decisive, or an Xbox-licensed headset ('Direct pairing to console'). The page should ask about platform first, as ChatGPT's follow-up question did, and add a 'Works wirelessly on Xbox: no' column.

findings.note: Even Microsoft's own headset gives Bluetooth for PC and mobile only, and links to the console through direct pairing. The page does not name the protocol. It supports the point that a generic 2.4 GHz dongle or Bluetooth will not reach an Xbox.
